article.title: Crystal 1.22.3 Patches Four Newly Disclosed Vulnerabilities, Including an HTTP Request-Smuggling Desync Bug and a Port-Truncation SSRF Bypass
article.summary: Crystal's November 13 patch release fixes four GitHub security advisories covering an HTTP chunked-encoding desync, a socket port-truncation SSRF bypass, an Enum.parse? stack write, and an IO::Delimited boundary bug.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

The Crystal programming language project released version 1.22.3 on November 13, 2026, a patch the [official release announcement](https://crystal-lang.org/2026/11/13/1.22.3-released/) says ships "important security patches, regression fixes, and normal bug fixes." Alongside the release, the project [published](https://github.com/crystal-lang/crystal/security/advisories/GHSA-5425-p3gq-r48v) four GitHub Security Advisories the same day, covering issues in the standard library's socket handling, HTTP chunked-transfer parsing, delimiter-based stream reading, and enum parsing. None of the four has been assigned a CVE identifier or a CVSS score in GitHub's advisory records.

## The four advisories

Two of the advisories carry a "medium" severity rating. The first, [GHSA-6q3x-6xhw-wfxp](https://github.com/crystal-lang/crystal/security/advisories/GHSA-6q3x-6xhw-wfxp), describes a bug in which opening a socket to a port number above 65535 could silently truncate to a 16-bit value and connect to the truncated port instead of raising an error — on affected systems, the advisory's own example shows a connection to port 73616 actually landing on port 8080. The advisory calls the impact an "SSRF port denylist bypass," since a check such as `port != 8080` would pass for 73616 while the connection goes to 8080 anyway. It attributes the root cause to how some C library implementations of `getaddrinfo` handle out-of-range ports, noting the targets `*-linux-gnu`, `*-windows-gnu` and `*-windows-msvc` were affected while `*-linux-musl` and `*-freebsd` were not. The advisory links a glibc bug tracker entry open since 2013 that, in the advisory's own words, "doesn't seem to be considered a vulnerability" by glibc's maintainers.

The second medium-severity advisory, [GHSA-5425-p3gq-r48v](https://github.com/crystal-lang/crystal/security/advisories/GHSA-5425-p3gq-r48v), covers an out-of-bounds stack write in `Enum.parse?` when processing input containing wide characters, which the advisory traces to a buffer-sizing optimization introduced in Crystal 1.22.0. GitHub classifies it under CWE-787 (Out-of-Bounds Write) and describes the impact as a possible memory-safety violation that "could potentially lead to data corruption on the stack" or, at minimum, a crash usable for denial of service. This advisory is the only one of the four that lists an explicit patched-version field pointing to 1.22.3; the Crystal maintainers credit Blacksmoke16 as the finder.

The two remaining advisories are rated "low." [GHSA-j97w-qwpv-7cfv](https://github.com/crystal-lang/crystal/security/advisories/GHSA-j97w-qwpv-7cfv) describes how `HTTP::ChunkedContent`'s chunk-size parser accepted negative hexadecimal values, causing two different read methods to disagree about where a chunked message ends — in the advisory's proof of concept, one method stops at byte position 14 and another at position 24, a 10-byte gap. GitHub's advisory calls the impact "HTTP request smuggling / CL-TE desync," explaining that a proxy reading with one method and a backend reading with another would disagree on where the next request begins. [GHSA-jgv7-2p84-pm39](https://github.com/crystal-lang/crystal/security/advisories/GHSA-jgv7-2p84-pm39) covers a related class of bug in `IO::Delimited`, where delimiter matching across a buffer boundary reached via `IO#peek` could cause the reader to recognize a delimiter that doesn't actually occur in the input. The advisory is more cautious about this one's real-world impact, stating: "We are not aware of any immediate vulnerability in the Crystal standard library. But there might be security implications for applications relying on `IO::Delimited` for message framing and protocol parsing." Both of these low-severity advisories credit the same reporter, bararchy, who also reported the socket port-truncation issue.

Neither the socket nor the two HTTP/IO advisories lists a value in GitHub's structured "patched versions" field, but each links a specific pull request as its patch — #17848, #17898 and #17916 respectively — and all three pull request numbers appear in [the 1.22.3 release's own changelog on GitHub](https://github.com/crystal-lang/crystal/releases/tag/1.22.3), under bug fixes tagged "security."

## HTTP parser hardening beyond the advisories

[The 1.22.3 release notes](https://github.com/crystal-lang/crystal/releases/tag/1.22.3) list three further security-tagged fixes in the same area that were not issued as separate advisories: rejecting control whitespace before a field value in HTTP headers, making sure a `close` token in the `Connection` header always closes the connection regardless of other values present, and validating the `Content-Length` header. The [announcement](https://crystal-lang.org/2026/11/13/1.22.3-released/) frames these together as fixes to "a couple of bugs in the HTTP message parser which previously accepted some invalid inputs," warning that invalid inputs "could potentially result in a protocol desync with a parser that interprets these invalid message in a different way," and says such inputs "now always result in an error." The announcement also credits the release with 14 changes since 1.22.2 from four contributors — a count the project reports itself rather than one independently verified by the Herald.

The cluster of HTTP-parsing fixes follows an [earlier Crystal advisory](https://github.com/crystal-lang/crystal/security/advisories/GHSA-wqh5-7w63-pm68), published April 16, 2026, that found the standard library's `HTTP::Server` was "prone to request smuggling" and was patched in version 1.20.0 — meaning this is at least the second round of request-smuggling-adjacent fixes to Crystal's HTTP stack in 2026.

## What We Don't Know

The cited sources do not say whether any of the four newly disclosed bugs has been exploited outside of the proof-of-concept code in the advisories themselves, nor do they give CVE identifiers or CVSS vector scores for any of the four. The Herald's prior coverage of [Crystal 1.22.0](/article/2026-10/15-crystal-1220-published-october-12-removes-processfork-exits-on-broken-pipe-writes-and-moves-aarch64-linux-to-tier-1) did not mention any of these issues, which were disclosed after that release shipped.
